content: Phlegmon is a condition characterized by a spreading, diffuse inflammatory process that involves the formation of purulent exudate or pus. The development of phlegmon is influenced by two primary factors: the virulence of the bacteria involved and the strength of the host's immune defense mechanisms. Phlegmon is most commonly caused by bacterial pathogens, including Staphylococci, Streptococci, Pneumococci, spore-forming anaerobes, and non-spore-forming anaerobes. Systemic symptoms of infection associated with phlegmon may include an elevated body temperature ranging from 38°C to 40°C, general fatigue, chills, excessive sweating, headache, and loss of appetite. During a physical examination, classic signs of inflammation may be observed. These include localized pain (dolor), increased local tissue temperature (calor), redness or hyperemia of the skin (rubor), tissue swelling that may have either well-defined or poorly defined borders (tumor), and impaired function of the affected area (functio laesa). The severity of the condition often correlates with the degree of systemic intoxication. The primary objective of treatment is to eliminate the underlying cause of the phlegmonous process to ensure effective resolution and to prevent recurrence. If the patient presents with a mild condition and there are signs of an inflammatory process without evidence of infiltrates, conservative treatment with antibiotics is typically sufficient.
